newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's truth probe exposing raw nerves.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's truth probe exposing raw nerves.

text.p: As South Africa's truth commission delves further into apartheid crime, more security force units are being implicated and divisive moral issues are being raised.
For the first time, senior police officers testifying before the commission identified the military special forces as being behind the assassination of anti-apartheid activists in 1986.

They said members of the secretive unit used their explosives expertise to kill one black leader and brought in two black Angolan agents to kill a leading member of the African National Congress and his wife.
The police this week also said that special forces soldiers used lethal injections to kill 10 black youths caught as they were leaving the country to join the ANC armed wing.
In an apparent bid to pre-empt the testimony, the defence forces last week invited journalists to make an unprecedented tour of a special forces base.
"We have nothing to hide," base commander Colonel Julius Engelbrecht said at the time. "We are not busy with any activities other than authorised activities."

Asked about the unit's past, Engelbrecht said: "The ANC was organised as a terrorist organisation. That was our perception, and we had to make sure that South Africa was a governable, safe area. We addressed the problem like that."
Many of the unit's members are black, and their original brief in the 1970s when the special forces were set up was to infiltrate the ANC and other black liberation groups.

Now a reconnaissance and fast reaction force, the unit was temporarily disbanded in 1993 along with other sections of the security forces deemed embarrassing to F.W. de Klerk's National Party, which was gearing up for the first all-race election in 1994.

The revelations before the truth commission this week have shown that the extra-judicial killing of government opponents during the 1980s was not confined to one or two police units such as the one led by former colonel Eugene de Kock.

De Kock, given two life terms and an additional 212 years in jail this week for a career of torture and murder, is among the dozens of security force officers now seeking amnesty from the truth commission.
But tension is building over the failure of any individual ANC member to approach the commission for amnesty.

Leaders of President Nelson Mandela's party have said there is no need to seek amnesty for what they did to bring down apartheid, but commission chairman Desmond Tutu retorted that the commission would serve no purpose if one side was to unilaterally declare itself blameless.

ANC Justice Minister Dullah Omar commented: "The ANC was engaged in a struggle for liberation which was a just struggle recognised to be so by the international community. Nothing that the truth commission does or what I do or what the government does is going to change that."
The National Party, which implemented apartheid in 1948 and began dismantling it in 1990, said Omar's attitude did not bode well for reconciliation.
"Individuals who have committed criminal acts or acts which infringe human rights, for whatever political cause, must face the consequences of those acts," the party said.

White parties to the right of the National Party have said the failure of ANC members to seek amnesty for killing civilians during their armed struggle confirmed their belief that the truth commission was a witch hunt against the apartheid security forces.
